--- title: "Surveillance and outbreak response" subtitle: "Where to sample, and what to do when something is already spreading" description: "Biodiversity-informed wildlife disease surveillance, and earlier outbreak response work on COVID-19 and mpox." categories: [Surveillance, One Health, Outbreak Response] toc: true execute: echo: false warning: false message: false --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} Placeholder page. Framing text is a draft. This page absorbs the former COVID-19 and mpox theme pages, which is why those sections are written in the past tense. Explainer notes for the papers are in `data/paper_notes/`. ::: Surveillance is a resource allocation problem before it is a laboratory one. Sampling wildlife is expensive, so the question is where a sample changes what we know. Outbreak response is the same question under time pressure. ## Wildlife disease surveillance **A protocol for biodiversity-informed wildlife disease surveillance.** *PLOS Ecosystems*, 2026. Host species distribution models set a biodiversity dose, uncertainty identifies where discovery sampling would help most, and balanced-acceptance sampling turns the result into field sites. Case studies on *Hantaviridae* and *Arenaviridae* in India and South Korea. Ongoing work extends this to outbreak settings, where the sampling frame has to be revised as an event unfolds. ## mpox Work from the 2022 outbreak and from the endemic range that preceded it. **Increased outbreaks of mpox highlight gaps in actual disease burden.** *International Journal of Infectious Diseases*, 2022. Two hypotheses for the global outbreak: growing synanthropic rodent populations in West and Central Africa, and an immunologically naive population 45 years after smallpox vaccination ended. **Community transmission of mpox in the United Kingdom.** *Eurosurveillance*, 2022. The first UK cases without travel history, described during the investigation, from work in the UK Health Security Agency outbreak surveillance team. The reservoir of mpox virus is still unidentified. Virus has been isolated from wild animals twice, and antibodies have been found in several further species. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

That work is finished. The papers are listed on the [publications page](/publications.html). ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} To add: the COVID-19 figure carried over from the old theme page, and a short account of the UKHSA surveillance work. :::
